categories.blurb: 第一個問題決定對方會給你罐頭答案還是真話。
把抽象答案逼成一個真實故事。
對方講完了，再往下一層。台灣人通常在這裡停。
問什麼行不通，比問什麼有用更能挖到真東西。
把觀念逼成「我明天可以做什麼」。
把對方講的整理回去讓他確認。
怎麼結束一個話題而不突兀。

questions.q: Let me set the stage for the conversation that we're going to have today.
questions.zh: 我先把今天這場對話的背景鋪一下。
questions.why: 開場先宣告「我要鋪背景」，等於當場跟對方買下三十秒的獨白時間，他知道現在不用急著接話。省掉「以為你問完了、其實還沒」的搶拍尷尬。
questions.pattern: Let me set the stage for [the conversation] that we're going to have [today].
questions.episode: Aishwarya Naresh Reganti + Kiriti Badam

questions.q: So, let's start with just the basics.
questions.zh: 那我們就從最基本的開始。
questions.why: just the basics 把起跑線壓到最低，替專家免除「講太淺很掉價」的顧慮，他才願意從頭講。同一句話也替聽眾建立共同背景。
questions.pattern: So, let's start with just [the basics].
questions.episode: The ultimate guide to Martech | Austin Hay (Reforge, Ramp, Runway)

questions.q: I want to start with a spicy question.
questions.zh: 我想用一個比較嗆的問題開場。
questions.why: 先幫問題貼上 spicy 的標籤，等於預告「這題不客氣」。對方有了心理準備就不會覺得被伏擊，反而等於被授權可以直說。
questions.pattern: I want to start with a [spicy] question.
questions.episode: Boris Cherny

questions.q: There's so much I want to talk to you about, but I want to start with a warm and fuzzy question.
questions.zh: 想跟你聊的東西太多了，不過我想先從一個溫馨一點的問題開始。
questions.why: 前半句先承認「題目很多」，讓對方知道第一題只是起點不是全部，不必把話一次講完；後半句用 warm and fuzzy 定調，把第一題的壓力降到最低。
questions.pattern: There's so much I want to talk to you about, but I want to start with [a warm and fuzzy question].
questions.episode: Inside Canva: Coaches not managers, giving away your Legos, and running profitably | Cameron Adams (co-founder and CPO)

questions.q: I want to use this conversation to basically help people understand this space deeply, but let's start with the basics.
questions.zh: 我想用這場對話讓大家真正搞懂這個領域，不過我們先從基本的開始。
questions.why: 一句話同時交代整場的目標（深入）跟這一刻的位置（從基本開始）。對方知道要往深講，但現在還不用跳到深水區。
questions.pattern: I want to use this conversation to basically help people understand [X] deeply, but let's start with the basics.
questions.episode: Why AI evals are the hottest new skill for product builders | Hamel Husain & Shreya Shankar (creators of the #1 eval course)

questions.q: I want to start with a phrase that came up again and again when I ask people what to talk to you about from your colleagues, and this phrase is conscious leadership.
questions.zh: 我想從一個詞開始。我問你同事該跟你聊什麼的時候，這個詞一直重複出現——conscious leadership。
questions.why: 把題目的來源掛在第三方身上（同事、反覆出現），問題就不是你的好奇而是既成事實，對方很難迴避。關鍵詞留到最後才丟，製造一個小懸念。
questions.pattern: I want to start with a phrase that came up again and again when I ask people [what to talk to you about], and this phrase is [X].
questions.episode: Becoming a conscious leader: Leading without fear, finding your life’s objective function, and getting better at vision and strategy | John Mark Nickels (Uber, Waymo, DoorDash)

questions.q: I want to start with just a big picture question.
questions.zh: 我想先問一個比較大方向的問題。
questions.why: big picture 這個標籤等於授權對方講抽象、講框架，不必先交代細節，也預告了細節留到後面。開場最省力的一種鋪陳。
questions.pattern: I want to start with just a [big picture] question.
questions.episode: Marc Andreessen: The real AI boom hasn’t even started yet

questions.q: I want to start by asking you a question that is on the minds of a lot of product managers is how to be less annoying as a product manager.
questions.zh: 我想先問一個很多 PM 心裡都有的問題：PM 要怎麼樣才不會那麼惹人嫌。
questions.why: 先說「這是很多人心裡的疑問」，一個可能冒犯的問題就變成群眾代表發問——對方是在回答一群人，不是被你挑釁。
questions.pattern: I want to start by asking you a question that is on the minds of a lot of [PMs], which is [X].
questions.episode: The things engineers are desperate for PMs to understand | Camille Fournier (author of “The Manager’s Path,” ex-CTO at Rent the Runway)

questions.q: I want to start with something that's very timely, something that's happening this week.
questions.zh: 我想從一件很即時的事開始，就是這禮拜正在發生的事。
questions.why: 用 timely 幫問題爭取插隊權——這題現在不問就過期了，對方不容易推說「這個晚點再談」。重複 something that's 也讓句子有節奏、順便替自己爭取想下一句的時間。
questions.pattern: I want to start with something that's very timely, something that's happening [this week].
questions.episode: Benjamin Mann

questions.q: I want to start with the elephant in the room, which I think the elephant is actually leaving the room because I think this is months ago at this point, but I'm still just really curious.
questions.zh: 我想從房間裡那頭大象開始講——雖然我覺得那頭象其實正在離場了，因為這都幾個月前的事了，但我還是很好奇。
questions.why: 先點名「大家都知道但沒人講的事」，再自己補一句「其實已經退燒」把火氣降下來，最後用 I'm still just really curious 把提問的理由歸給好奇而不是究責。
questions.pattern: I want to start with the elephant in the room, ... but I'm still just really curious.
questions.episode: Inside OpenAI | Logan Kilpatrick (head of developer relations)

questions.q: What I want to start with is to give us a little insight into how you became what you became.
questions.zh: 我想先從一件事開始：讓我們稍微了解一下，你是怎麼變成今天的你的。
questions.why: 用 give us a little insight 取代「請你自我介紹」，把題目框成分享一點內幕而不是報履歷，對方講出來的會是故事而不是條列。
questions.pattern: What I want to start with is to give us a little insight into [how you became what you became].
questions.episode: How to find hidden growth opportunities in your product | Albert Cheng (Duolingo, Grammarly, Chess.com)

questions.q: Let me start with just setting a little context, and for folks that aren't super familiar with what is a marketplace business, they hear this term marketplace company, what's the simplest way to understand what makes a company a marketplace company and a marketplace business?
questions.zh: 我先鋪一點背景。對不太熟「平台型生意」的人來說，他們聽到 marketplace company 這個詞，最簡單要怎麼理解一家公司算是 marketplace？
questions.why: 把「我不懂」外包給 folks that aren't super familiar，專家就不會覺得你在測他的程度。the simplest way to understand 又直接指定了答案的難度上限。
questions.pattern: Let me start with just setting a little context, and for folks that aren't super familiar with [X], what's the simplest way to understand [X]?
questions.episode: How marketplaces win: Liquidity, growth levers, quality, and more | Benjamin Lauzier (Lyft, Thumbtack, Reforge)

questions.q: I want to start with just trying to understand and help people understand why is it so freaking hard to build a durable, lasting consumer product and in particular a social consumer product.
questions.zh: 我想先從搞懂一件事開始，也幫大家搞懂：為什麼要做出一個能撐很久的消費型產品——尤其是社群產品——會那麼難？
questions.why: understand and help people understand 這個雙層說法把「我想知道」跟「大家想知道」綁在一起，問題就有了公共性。so freaking hard 的口語強度則在邀請對方講真話而不是官腔。
questions.pattern: I want to start with just trying to understand and help people understand why is it so hard to [X].
questions.episode: Snapchat CEO: Why distribution has become the most important moat | Evan Spiegel

questions.q: Okay, so Dylan, I want to start by just checking in on how you're doing.
questions.zh: 好，Dylan，我想先關心一下你最近好嗎。
questions.why: 先叫名字再 checking in，把第一題設定成關心而不是提問。對方通常會自己交代近況，你等於免費拿到一段脈絡當後面的引子。
questions.pattern: Okay, so [name], I want to start by just checking in on how you're doing.
questions.episode: Dylan Field live at Config: Intuition, simplicity, and the future of design

questions.q: Can you maybe make it even more concrete?
questions.zh: 可以再講得更具體一點嗎？
questions.why: 一句話把抽象打回去要細節。maybe 讓語氣不像糾正，even more 又先肯定對方剛剛已經講得不錯、只是還能再往下一層。
questions.pattern: Can you maybe make it even more concrete?
questions.episode: Unorthodox frameworks for growing your product, career, and impact | Bangaly Kaba (YouTube, Instagram, Facebook, Instacart)

questions.q: What's an example of that, just to make it more concrete for us?
questions.zh: 可以舉個例子嗎？讓我們比較具體一點。
questions.why: 先要例子，再用 just to make it more concrete for us 補上理由——把要求包成「我們需要」，對方不會解讀成「你剛剛講得不夠好」。
questions.pattern: What's an example of that, just to make it more concrete for us?
questions.episode: Why we’re at the beginning of the AI hardware boom | Caitlin Kalinowski (ex–OpenAI, Meta, Apple)

questions.q: What's a tactical tip or two that you can suggest to a founder or product manager to help them contain the design process while also achieving these outcomes that you're describing?
questions.zh: 你會給創辦人或 PM 哪一兩個實際做得到的小訣竅，讓他們既能把設計流程收斂好、又能達到你剛講的那些結果？
questions.why: a tip or two 幫對方把答案量化成一到兩個，他就不會發散。再指定對象跟目標，答案自動變成可執行的建議而不是理念。
questions.pattern: What's a tactical tip or two that you can suggest to [a founder or PM] to help them [X] while also achieving [these outcomes]?
questions.episode: 35 years of product design wisdom from Apple, Disney, Pinterest, and beyond | Bob Baxley

questions.q: Just to leave people with a tactical piece of advice, say they are like, "Oh man, I need a coach," do you have any advice for how to find a coach?
questions.zh: 想留一個實際可用的建議給大家——假設有人心裡想「天啊我需要一個教練」，你會怎麼建議他去找？
questions.why: say they are like 後面直接演一段內心話，把抽象的「聽眾」變成一個具體的人跟具體處境。對方會針對那個處境回答，而不是講原則。
questions.pattern: Just to leave people with a tactical piece of advice, say they are like, "[內心話]," do you have any advice for how to [X]?
questions.episode: How to own your career growth and become a powerful product leader | Deb Liu, Ancestry (ex-Facebook, PayPal)

questions.q: Very tactically, what do you recommend people do?
questions.zh: 講得很實際一點，你會建議大家怎麼做？
questions.why: 把 tactically 提到句首當開關，一開口就宣告「接下來不要理論」。七個字就能把一段哲學拉回動作層。
questions.pattern: Very tactically, what do you recommend people do?
questions.episode: How to discover your superpowers, own your story, and unlock personal growth | Donna Lichaw (author of The Leader’s Journey)

questions.q: Talk about when you think about what is good taste, good judgment, what is that concretely?
questions.zh: 聊一下，你說的好品味、好判斷力，具體到底是什麼？
questions.why: 把對方用的抽象詞原封不動唸回去，再加 concretely 逼他定義。他沒辦法再用同一個詞解釋同一個詞。
questions.pattern: Talk about when you think about [抽象詞], what is that concretely?
questions.episode: OpenAI Codex lead on the new shape of product work | Andrew Ambrosino

questions.q: So what is a vision concretely as a document in your experience?
questions.zh: 所以以你的經驗來說，願景具體作為一份文件，長什麼樣？
questions.why: concretely as a document 幫抽象概念指定了一個實體形式——你要的不是定義，是一份可以打開來看的東西，對方只能描述真實產物。
questions.pattern: So what is [X] concretely as [a document] in your experience?
questions.episode: Crafting a compelling product vision | Ebi Atawodi (YouTube, Netflix, Uber)

questions.q: When you say data preparation, what's an example to make that real and concrete for us to understand?
questions.zh: 你說的「資料準備」，可以舉個例子讓我們具體理解嗎？
questions.why: When you say 先把對方剛用的術語隔離出來，不否定也不假裝懂。接著只要一個例子，比問「那是什麼意思」少了質疑感。
questions.pattern: When you say [術語], what's an example to make that real and concrete for us to understand?
questions.episode: Al Engineering 101 with Chip Huyen (Nvidia, Stanford, Netflix)

questions.q: What's the first step that you recommend for people to go down?
questions.zh: 你會建議大家的第一步是什麼？
questions.why: 只要 the first step、不要整套流程。對方無法丟一個大架構搪塞，聽的人也拿到一個明天就能做的動作。
questions.pattern: What's the first step that you recommend for people to go down?
questions.episode: The ultimate guide to adding a PLG motion | Hila Qu (Reforge, GitLab)

questions.q: To make that last point a little more concrete, what's an example of that?
questions.zh: 為了讓你剛剛那個點更具體一點，可以舉個例子嗎？
questions.why: that last point 精準指回剛講的那一段，對方不會整段重講。a little 又讓要求聽起來只是微調，不是打回重寫。
questions.pattern: To make that last point a little more concrete, what's an example of that?
questions.episode: Developing a growth model + marketplace growth strategy | Dan Hockenmaier (Faire, Thumbtack, Reforge)

questions.q: Do you have any tactical advice for someone that is not good at this for how to actually say something uncomfortable?
questions.zh: 對於本來就不擅長這件事的人，你有沒有什麼實際的建議，教他怎麼真的把難講的話講出口？
questions.why: 指定對象是「本來就不擅長的人」，答案的難度上限被鎖死，對方不能給只有高手做得到的建議。actually say 又把答案逼到「真的開口那一刻」。
questions.pattern: Do you have any tactical advice for someone that is not good at this for how to actually [X]?
questions.episode: Lessons from scaling Stripe | Claire Hughes Johnson (former COO of Stripe)

questions.q: Is it just in your mind you're like, "I'm going to have fun with this," or is there something tactically people can do to make something fun?
questions.zh: 這只是你心裡想「我要玩得開心一點」而已，還是說有什麼實際做法可以讓事情變好玩？
questions.why: 給一個二選一，而且故意把第一個選項寫得空泛。對方為了不落入空泛，就會選第二個並交出做法——把觀念逼成做法最有效的一招。
questions.pattern: Is it just in your mind you're like, "[心態]," or is there something tactically people can do to [X]?
questions.episode: Becoming more strategic, navigating difficult colleagues, harnessing founder mode, and more | Anneka Gupta (Chief Product Officer at Rubrik)

questions.q: How do you actually kind of tactically operationalize that?
questions.zh: 那實際上要怎麼把它變成日常在運作的東西？
questions.why: operationalize 指的是「變成制度、變成每天在跑的流程」，比 how do you do it 更難敷衍——對方必須交代誰做、多久做一次。
questions.pattern: How do you actually kind of tactically operationalize that?
questions.episode: Building a culture of excellence | David Singleton (CTO of Stripe)

questions.q: If people listening are also sold and want to build a company this way, what can they do?
questions.zh: 如果正在聽的人也被說服了，想照這個方式建一家公司，他們可以怎麼做？
questions.why: 先假設對方已經說服成功（are also sold），跳過辯論直接問下一步。他就不會再花時間補論證，而是給行動。
questions.pattern: If people listening are also sold and want to [X], what can they do?
questions.episode: Reflections on a movement | Eric Ries (creator of the Lean Startup methodology)

questions.q: Or is there a story of something where you just shipped something that shows this customer obsession to make it even more concrete for listeners?
questions.zh: 或者有沒有一個實際例子，你們出過什麼東西，能體現這種對客戶的執著，讓聽的人更有畫面？
questions.why: 要的是 story 而不是 example，對方會給時間、人物、結果，資訊密度高很多。for listeners 又把要求轉成替第三方著想。
questions.pattern: Or is there a story of something where you just [做了X] that shows [這個特質] to make it even more concrete for listeners?
questions.episode: Relentless curiosity, radical accountability, and HubSpot’s winning growth formula | Christopher Miller (VP of Product, Growth and AI)

questions.q: So what I'm hearing is find a problem that can be solved, find a problem, a pain point for yourself or someone, and then end-to-end fully solve that problem.
questions.zh: 所以我聽到的是：找一個解得掉的問題，一個你自己或別人真的會痛的點，然後從頭到尾把它徹底解決。
questions.why: what I'm hearing is 把對方一長串的話濃縮成一句祈使句，等於幫他把觀點寫成標題。對方通常會接受你的版本並順著往下講。
questions.pattern: So what I'm hearing is [濃縮後的主張].
questions.episode: Building Lovable: $10M ARR in 60 days with 15 people | Anton Osika (co-founder and CEO)

questions.q: And a big part of this is distribution, essentially, breaking through the noise is what I'm hearing?
questions.zh: 所以這裡很大一塊其實是通路——重點是怎麼殺出重圍，我這樣理解對嗎？
questions.why: 把 is what I'm hearing 挪到句尾，前半句就能用肯定語氣講，聽起來像在補完對方的話；結尾才輕輕把確認權交還。比一開頭就問「你是說⋯嗎」更不打斷。
questions.pattern: [你的濃縮版本] is what I'm hearing?
questions.episode: Sequoia CEO coach: Why it’s never been easier to start a company, and never been harder to scale one | Brian Halligan (co-founder, HubSpot)

questions.q: So you intentionally set that announcement up to be controversial is what I'm hearing?
questions.zh: 所以你是刻意把那則公告弄得有爭議性的，我這樣聽對嗎？
questions.why: 把對方沒明說的動機（intentionally）講出來，再用 is what I'm hearing 收尾。他若否認會主動補說明，若默認你就拿到一個他自己不會主動講的重點。
questions.pattern: So you intentionally [做了X] is what I'm hearing?
questions.episode: “Dumbest idea I’ve heard” to $100M ARR: Inside the rise of Gamma | Grant Lee (CEO)

questions.q: Okay, let me try to reflect back some of the advice I've been hearing about how to shift a company to be successful in this new world, and let me see if I'm missing anything that you think is really important.
questions.zh: 好，我試著把剛剛聽到的建議整理回去——關於一家公司要怎麼調整才能在這個新局裡活得好——你看我有沒有漏掉什麼你覺得很重要的。
questions.why: reflect back 先宣告要複誦，再用 see if I'm missing anything 把球丟回去。最精巧的是它把「我可能聽錯」寫成「我可能漏掉」，對方補充時不必否定你。
questions.pattern: Okay, let me try to reflect back [我聽到的X], and let me see if I'm missing anything that you think is really important.
questions.episode: How we restructured Airtable’s entire org for AI | Howie Liu (co-founder and CEO)

questions.q: Just to close the loop on this advice around getting better at vision and strategy, if I were to reflect back what I'm hearing its be very self-aware about what you are not strong at, say openness.
questions.zh: 為了把「怎麼把願景跟策略做得更好」這段收個尾——如果我把聽到的整理回去，就是：要非常清楚自己哪裡不強，比方說開放性。
questions.why: close the loop 宣告這是收尾不是新問題；if I were to reflect back 用假設語氣，先替自己的複述留了退路，對方要糾正的成本趨近於零。
questions.pattern: Just to close the loop on this advice around [X], if I were to reflect back what I'm hearing it's [Y].
questions.episode: Improve strategy, influence, and decision-making by understanding your brain | Evan LaPointe (founder of CORE Sciences)

questions.q: What I'm hearing is step one is just get your kind of peer leaders aligned behind something that may not obviously be something your leaders want you to do, is that right?
questions.zh: 我聽到的是，第一步就是先把跟你平行的那些主管拉到同一邊，即使那件事表面上未必是你老闆想要你做的——是這樣嗎？
questions.why: 複述時自己加上 step one，等於把對方的話重新編號成流程；結尾補 is that right? 讓這個加工得到他的授權。
questions.pattern: What I'm hearing is step one is just [X], is that right?
questions.episode: How to sell your ideas and rise within your company | Casey Winters, Eventbrite

questions.q: So correct me if I'm wrong, but kind of the advice you're sharing is there's less opportunity in just generating tons of blog posts that just have a bunch of content.
questions.zh: 我理解錯就糾正我——你分享的建議大概是說，光是狂產一堆有內容的部落格文章，機會已經比較小了。
questions.why: correct me if I'm wrong 先把否決權交出去，你就可以放膽講一個比對方原話更銳利的版本。他若不同意會自己修正，你反而拿到更精準的說法。
questions.pattern: So correct me if I'm wrong, but kind of the advice you're sharing is [X].
questions.episode: Rethinking SEO in the age of AI | Eli Schwartz (SEO advisor, author)

questions.q: And correct me if I'm wrong, but you guys have moved away from that approach.
questions.zh: 我說錯的話糾正我——你們後來已經不走那條路了。
questions.why: 用陳述句而不是問句丟出推測，對方只要點頭或修正，比問句推進得更快；前半句是安全氣囊，讓你猜錯也不失分。
questions.pattern: And correct me if I'm wrong, but [你的推論陳述].
questions.episode: Gustav Söderström

questions.q: Let me just try to summarize what you shared, this five step framework.
questions.zh: 我試著把你剛分享的整理一下，這個五步驟的架構。
questions.why: try to 讓複述變成一次嘗試而不是定論；把內容當場命名成 this five step framework，等於替對方的說法取了一個好記的名字。
questions.pattern: Let me just try to summarize what you shared, this [five step framework].
questions.episode: The power of strategic narrative | Andy Raskin

questions.q: I'm going to summarize what you just shared, which is awesome.
questions.zh: 我來把你剛剛講的整理一下，超棒的。
questions.why: 用 I'm going to 而不是 can I 直接取得發言權，後面 which is awesome 順手給個肯定，讓「我要接手講幾句」聽起來像稱讚而不是打斷。
questions.pattern: I'm going to summarize what you just shared, which is awesome.
questions.episode: Breaking the rules of growth: Why Shopify bans KPIs, optimizes for churn, prioritizes intuition, and builds toward a 100-year vision | Archie Abrams (VP Product, Head of Growth at Shopify)

questions.q: So just to summarize the audit that you do, I wrote some notes as you were talking, and maybe we can keep going from that point.
questions.zh: 我把你做的那套盤點整理一下——你在講的時候我有做筆記——然後我們也許可以從那邊接下去。
questions.why: 講出「我有做筆記」，複述就有了憑據，對方會更認真聽你的版本。最後 keep going from that point 直接把摘要當成下一段的起跑線。
questions.pattern: So just to summarize [X], I wrote some notes as you were talking, and maybe we can keep going from that point.
questions.episode: The ultimate guide to adding a PLG motion | Hila Qu (Reforge, GitLab)

questions.q: So, just to summarize, the main benefits are focuses you, lines, creates a cadence and creates a learning cycle.
questions.zh: 所以整理一下，主要的好處是讓你聚焦、對齊、建立節奏，還有形成學習循環。
questions.why: 把對方散落各處的說法收成四個並列動詞，短、平行、好記。摘要的價值就在這裡：你交回去的版本要比原話更容易被複述。
questions.pattern: So, just to summarize, the main benefits are [A], [B], [C] and [D].
questions.episode: The ultimate guide to OKRs | Christina Wodtke (Stanford)

questions.q: Okay, let me take this opportunity to try to summarize what I've learned from you so far in terms of what you guys have figured out about creating incredible product leaders.
questions.zh: 好，我趁這個機會整理一下到目前為止從你這邊學到的，關於你們在培養頂尖產品主管上摸索出來的東西。
questions.why: take this opportunity 幫這段摘要找到時機上的正當性——不是打斷，是把握機會。so far 又留了伏筆：後面還有，這只是中場整理。
questions.pattern: Okay, let me take this opportunity to try to summarize what I've learned from you so far in terms of [X].
questions.episode: How Revolut trains world-class product managers: The “local CEO” model, raw intellect over experience, and a cultural obsession with building wow products | Dmitry Zlokazov (Head of Product)

questions.q: What I'm hearing is instead of AI being baked into SaaS tools, what you're predicting here is the SaaS tools will run within Codex or Claude Code?
questions.zh: 我聽到的是，與其說 AI 被塞進 SaaS 工具裡，你在這裡預測的其實是 SaaS 工具會跑在 Codex 或 Claude Code 之內？
questions.why: 用 instead of A, what you're predicting is B 的對照句型，把對方的觀點放在一個他沒說過的對立面旁邊，輪廓一下子清楚。順便把他的說法升格成「預測」。
questions.pattern: What I'm hearing is instead of [A], what you're predicting here is [B]?
questions.episode: The AI paradox: More automation, more humans, more work | Dan Shipper

questions.q: So what you're saying is not only is there going to be this big opportunity to grow, if you don't take advantage of it, somebody in your space will.
questions.zh: 所以你的意思是，這不只是一個很大的成長機會——你不抓，同業就會抓走。
questions.why: 複述時把對方的正面主張補上反面後果（你不做、別人會做），語氣加重了，但責任還掛在對方身上，因為開頭是 what you're saying is。
questions.pattern: So what you're saying is not only [A], if you don't [X], somebody will.
questions.episode: Brian Balfour: 10 lessons on career, growth, and life

questions.q: Is there anything else along the lines of this specific type of feedback that is worth sharing before we move on to a different type of feedback?
questions.zh: 在我們換到另一種回饋之前，關於這一類回饋，還有什麼值得補充的嗎？
questions.why: 先開補充的門、再宣告換題。順序是關鍵：先問「還有嗎」等於承認這段還沒榨乾，對方就算被切斷也不會覺得被打斷。
questions.pattern: Is there anything else along the lines of [this topic] that is worth sharing before we move on to [next topic]?
questions.episode: Scripts for difficult conversations: Giving hard feedback, navigating defensiveness, the three questions you should end every meeting with, more | Alisa Cohn (executive coach)

questions.q: Let me ask you one more question before we shift a whole different topic, hint, hint, AI.
questions.zh: 在我們換到一個完全不同的主題之前，我再問你一個問題——提示一下，是 AI。
questions.why: 先宣告「只剩一題」，對方會把最好的留在這一題。hint, hint 又先預告下一段主題，讓轉場變成期待而不是斷裂。
questions.pattern: Let me ask you one more question before we shift a whole different topic, hint, hint, [next topic].
questions.episode: I’ve run 75+ businesses. Here’s why you’re probably chasing the wrong idea. | Andrew Wilkinson (co‑founder of Tiny)

questions.q: One last question about the CPO role, and then I want to shift a bit to just product management and growth.
questions.zh: 關於 CPO 這個角色，最後問一題，然後我想稍微轉到產品管理跟成長。
questions.why: 「最後一題 + 下一站」塞在同一句，等於同時關門跟開門。對方回答時心裡已經在準備下一段，接得順。
questions.pattern: One last question about [X], and then I want to shift a bit to [Y].
questions.episode: How to sell your ideas and rise within your company | Casey Winters, Eventbrite

questions.q: Let me ask one more quick question on strategy and then I want to move on to career stuff.
questions.zh: 策略這塊我再快問一題，然後想接到職涯的部分。
questions.why: quick 是給對方的時間承諾，答案自然會短。跟「最後一題＋下一站」是同一招但更輕，適合已經聊很久、需要提速的時候。
questions.pattern: Let me ask one more quick question on [X] and then I want to move on to [Y].
questions.episode: Jackie Bavaro on getting better at product strategy, what exactly is strategy, PM pitfalls to avoid, advancing your career, getting into management, and much more

questions.q: One last question before we move on to the next step.
questions.zh: 在進到下一步之前，最後一個問題。
questions.why: 最短的一種收尾件。它同時做兩件事：關掉這一段的無限延伸，並提醒對方整場對話是有步驟的。
questions.pattern: One last question before we move on to the next step.
questions.episode: Customer-led growth | Georgiana Laudi (Forget The Funnel)

questions.q: Is there anything else along this thread before we move on to a different topic, anything else you want to share before we close out this chapter?
questions.zh: 這條線上還有什麼要補的嗎？在我們換題之前，還有什麼想分享的，好把這一章收起來？
questions.why: 同一個意思問兩次，第二次改用 chapter 這個比喻，把剛剛那段封裝成一個單位，暗示「講完就不回頭了」。對方通常會把壓箱的東西拿出來。
questions.pattern: Is there anything else along this thread before we move on to a different topic, anything else you want to share before we close out this chapter?
questions.episode: The creator of WordPress opens up about becoming an internet villain, why he’s taking a stand, and the future of open source | Matt Mullenweg (founder and CEO, Automattic)

questions.q: Let's shift topics and talk about product strategy.
questions.zh: 我們換個主題，來聊產品策略。
questions.why: 最乾脆的轉場：宣告換題＋直接指定新題，沒有鋪陳。上一段明顯已經收完的時候，硬轉反而俐落。
questions.pattern: Let's shift topics and talk about [X].
questions.episode: Mastering product strategy and growing as a PM | Maggie Crowley (Toast, Drift, Tripadvisor)

questions.q: Okay, let me zoom out a bit and I want to move on to a different topic.
questions.zh: 好，我拉遠一點看，然後想換到另一個主題。
questions.why: zoom out 是轉場的緩衝墊——先把鏡頭從細節拉遠，再換題就不會像硬切。中文裡我們常常直接說「那我們換個話題」，少了這一層。
questions.pattern: Okay, let me zoom out a bit and I want to move on to a different topic.
questions.episode: We replaced our sales team with 20 AI agents—here’s what happened | Jason Lemkin (SaaStr)

questions.q: Any last piece of wisdom to leave listeners with around The JOLT Effect before we move on to The Challenger Sale?
questions.zh: 在我們轉到《挑戰者銷售》之前，關於《JOLT 效應》還有什麼最後的智慧想留給聽眾的嗎？
questions.why: last piece of wisdom 把「補充」升格成「壓軸」，對方會挑最好的講而不是隨便補。leave listeners with 又把對象換成第三方——他不是在幫你收尾，是在給聽眾禮物。
questions.pattern: Any last piece of wisdom to leave listeners with around [X] before we move on to [Y]?
questions.episode: The surprising truth about what closes deals: Insights from 2.5m sales conversations | Matt Dixon (author of The Challenger Sale and The JOLT Effect)

questions.q: Let's transition to the third area I wanted to spend some time on, which is growth.
questions.zh: 我們轉到我想花點時間聊的第三塊——成長。
questions.why: 給轉場編號（the third area），聽的人立刻知道整場是有結構的、現在走到哪。編號也讓你可以合理地結束前一段，因為第二段「已經講完了」。
questions.pattern: Let's transition to the [third] area I wanted to spend some time on, which is [X].
questions.episode: Inside Linear: Building with taste, craft, and focus | Karri Saarinen (co-founder, designer, CEO)

questions.q: I have a couple of more coaching questions before we move on to a few other topics.
questions.zh: 在換到別的主題之前，我還有幾個關於教練的問題。
questions.why: 先公告「還有幾題」，對方就知道這一段還沒結束、不用把話全部塞進下一個回答，節奏會穩下來。
questions.pattern: I have a couple of more [X] questions before we move on to a few other topics.
questions.episode: How to unlock your product leadership skills | Ken Norton, Ex-Google

questions.q: I'd love to transition in to talk about investing a little bit before we get to our exciting lightning round.
questions.zh: 在進到快問快答之前，我想轉過來稍微聊一下投資。
questions.why: 一句話宣告兩層結構：下一段是投資，再下一段就要收尾了。對方能自己分配剩下的力氣。
questions.pattern: I'd love to transition in to talk about [X] a little bit before we get to [the closing segment].
questions.episode: Gokul Rajaram on designing your product development process, when and how to hire your first PM, a playbook for hiring leaders, getting ahead in you career, how to get started angel investing, more

questions.q: Is there any other ones you want to share before we move on to getting better at speaking on the spot?
questions.zh: 在我們轉到「怎麼把臨場說話練好」之前，還有其他想分享的嗎？
questions.why: 把下一段主題直接寫進轉場問句裡，對方補充的時候就會自動避開下一段會講到的東西，省掉重複。
questions.pattern: Is there any other ones you want to share before we move on to [next topic]?
questions.episode: How to speak more confidently and persuasively | Matt Abrahams (professor, podcast host, author, speaker)

questions.q: Just to close the loop here, one takeaway here that I think is really interesting is that you can fail in a job and things will be okay.
questions.zh: 這裡先把這一段收起來——我覺得有一個很有意思的收穫：你可以在一份工作上失敗，然後一切還是會沒事。
questions.why: close the loop 宣告收尾，接著自己提煉一個 takeaway 當結論。主持人替段落下結論，對話才有段落感；對方若不同意會補充，反而更好。
questions.pattern: Just to close the loop here, one takeaway here that I think is really interesting is that [X].
questions.episode: 35 years of product design wisdom from Apple, Disney, Pinterest, and beyond | Bob Baxley

questions.q: Anything else before we move on to number two?
questions.zh: 在進到第二點之前，還有什麼要補的嗎？
questions.why: 八個字完成一次收尾：確認補充＋標記進度。清單式的對話裡最好用，因為每次轉場都在提醒大家還剩幾點。
questions.pattern: Anything else before we move on to number [two]?
questions.episode: Elena Verna on how B2B growth is changing, product-led growth, product-led sales, why you should go freemium not trial, what features to make free, and much more

questions.q: Is there an example of that?
questions.zh: 有沒有一個實際的例子？
questions.why: 追問的最小單位。對方講完一段抽象論述後，不評論、不接話、直接要例子——六個字就把「聽起來很有道理」推到「拿證據出來」。短到不像質疑，所以幾乎不會踩雷。
questions.pattern: Is there an example of that?
questions.episode: How to drive word of mouth | Nilan Peiris (CPO of Wise)

questions.q: Is there an example that can make this even more real of a company or a product?
questions.zh: 有沒有哪個例子可以讓這件事更具體一點——某間公司或某個產品？
questions.why: 「make this even more real」把要求包裝成「幫聽眾理解」，不是「我不信你」。後半句 of a company or a product 先幫對方縮小搜尋範圍，對方不用從零想起，答得出來的機率大增。
questions.pattern: Is there an example that can make this even more real of a [公司／產品／專案]?
questions.episode: The ultimate guide to JTBD | Bob Moesta (co-creator of the framework)

questions.q: To close the loop on this piece of advice, is there an example you could share to make this super concrete for folks?
questions.zh: 為了把這個建議收尾收乾淨，有沒有一個例子可以分享，讓大家真的搞懂它長什麼樣？
questions.why: 「To close the loop on this piece of advice」先宣告這是收尾動作，不是開新戰場——對方知道再回答一輪就結束，比較願意給料。最後 for folks 把受益者從自己換成第三方。
questions.pattern: To close the loop on [主題], is there an example you could share to make this super concrete for folks?
questions.episode: A guide to difficult conversations, building high-trust teams, and designing a life you love | Rachel Lockett

questions.q: When you say high standards, is there something you could share that gives us an example of what you mean there? Because a lot of people think they have high standards and they don't.
questions.zh: 你說的「高標準」，可以舉個例子說明你指的是什麼嗎？因為很多人都以為自己標準很高，其實沒有。
questions.why: 第二句是關鍵：他不是說「我不懂」，而是說「這個詞被濫用了」。把要例子的理由外部化成一個公認現象，對方會覺得自己是在跟他一起對抗模糊，而不是被抽考。
questions.pattern: When you say [抽象詞], is there something you could share that gives us an example of what you mean there? Because a lot of people think they [X] and they don't.
questions.episode: Why experts writing AI evals is creating the fastest-growing companies in history | Brendan Foody (CEO of Mercor)

questions.q: Then, is there an example of a feature or product that went through this that you could share? If nothing comes to mind, that's okay.
questions.zh: 那有沒有哪個功能或產品實際走過這套流程、可以拿出來講的？想不到也沒關係。
questions.why: 後面那句「想不到也沒關係」是專業訪談者的標準配備：先給對方一個免責出口，對方就不必為了面子硬掰。弔詭的是，壓力一拿掉，人反而更容易想起真的例子。
questions.pattern: Is there an example of [X] that you could share? If nothing comes to mind, that's okay.
questions.episode: How to ask the right questions, project confidence, and win over skeptics | Paige Costello (Asana, Intercom, Intuit)

questions.q: Is there an example that comes to mind of someone that did this really well? I don't know. I know it's hard to think of just an example off the top of your head, but does anything come to mind?
questions.zh: 有沒有想到誰把這件事做得特別好的例子？我知道要臨場想例子很難，但有沒有什麼浮上來的？
questions.why: 第一次問完不放棄，而是把門檻降低再問一次：先承認「臨場想很難」（幫對方找好台階），再改用最低要求的說法 does anything come to mind。同一個問題問兩次而不顯得逼問，靠的就是中間那句體諒。
questions.pattern: Is there an example that comes to mind of someone that did this really well? I know it's hard to think of just an example off the top of your head, but does anything come to mind?
questions.episode: Navigating comms and PR | Lulu Cheng Meservey (Substack, Activision Blizzard)

questions.q: Is there an example of that gone wrong that you can share? Whether it's a company you've worked at or a company you've seen do it badly.
questions.zh: 有沒有做壞掉的例子可以講？不管是你待過的公司，還是你看別人做砸的。
questions.why: 問失敗案例最怕對方要自曝其短。第二句給了兩個選項：你自己的，或你看到別人的。對方可以選安全的那個回答，門檻直接減半，而你照樣拿到一個真實案例。
questions.pattern: Is there an example of that gone wrong that you can share? Whether it's a company you've worked at or a company you've seen do it badly.
questions.episode: Manik Gupta (ex-CPO Uber, Google Maps) on how to build consumer apps, why it’s useful to be optimistic about technology, creating inflections in your PM career, the changing CPO role, and more

questions.q: Is there an example of something that broke that would be illustrative of what you're describing?
questions.zh: 有沒有哪個東西壞掉的例子，剛好能說明你講的狀況？
questions.why: 不問「例子」而問「壞掉的例子」。故障、事故、翻車這類事件天生有時間、有細節、有情緒，比成功案例好回想也好講——所以這是最容易撬出具體故事的一種要法。
questions.pattern: Is there an example of something that broke that would be illustrative of what you're describing?
questions.episode: Breaking the rules of growth: Why Shopify bans KPIs, optimizes for churn, prioritizes intuition, and builds toward a 100-year vision | Archie Abrams (VP Product, Head of Growth at Shopify)

questions.q: That's such a cool simple way of thinking about this. Is there an example from your work that might illustrate some of this from a project you worked on or a product you built?
questions.zh: 這個思考方式又簡單又漂亮。有沒有你自己工作上的例子可以說明——某個你做過的專案或某個你打造過的產品？
questions.why: 先給一句真心的肯定當緩衝，再要例子。後半刻意把範圍限縮到「你自己做過的」，避免對方拿業界通例敷衍你；再列兩個容器（專案／產品）讓對方好對號入座。
questions.pattern: Is there an example from your work that might illustrate some of this from a project you worked on or a product you built?
questions.episode: Becoming more strategic, navigating difficult colleagues, harnessing founder mode, and more | Anneka Gupta (Chief Product Officer at Rubrik)

questions.q: Is there an example that maybe worked really well or maybe didn't work?
questions.zh: 有沒有哪個例子，做起來效果很好、或者其實沒成功的？
questions.why: 一次開兩個門：成功的或失敗的都收。對方不必先判斷「我該給正面還是負面案例」，回想的阻力最小；而且暗示了你不是只想聽好聽的。
questions.pattern: Is there an example that maybe worked really well or maybe didn't work?
questions.episode: How Block is becoming the most AI-native enterprise in the world | Dhanji R. Prasanna

questions.q: Is there an example of that that comes to mind of someone that did that incorrectly or wasted a lot of time?
questions.zh: 有沒有想到誰把這件事做錯、或白白浪費了很多時間的例子？
questions.why: 把主角設成第三人（someone），對方談的是別人的失誤，講起來沒有心理負擔。而且「做錯」和「浪費時間」是兩個很具體的檢索線索，比抽象地問「反例」好回想得多。
questions.pattern: Is there an example of that that comes to mind of someone that did that incorrectly or wasted a lot of time?
questions.episode: The future of AI in software development | Inbal Shani (CPO of GitHub)

questions.q: Is there an example of that or a story of that happening that you think about?
questions.zh: 有沒有這樣的例子、或是你常想起的某個實際發生過的故事？
questions.why: example 和 story 並列，等於同時給了兩種難度：講不出「代表性案例」的人，通常講得出「一個故事」。結尾 that you think about 把要求降到「你腦中常出現的那個就行」。
questions.pattern: Is there an example of that or a story of that happening that you think about?
questions.episode: 4 questions Shreyas Doshi wishes he’d asked himself sooner | Former PM leader at Stripe, Twitter, Google

questions.q: Is there an example of a good success metric that just comes to mind to make this a little bit concrete for people?
questions.zh: 有沒有哪個好的成功指標的例子剛好浮上來，可以讓大家比較有畫面？
questions.why: just comes to mind 是壓力消音器：明說「不用認真找、想到什麼算什麼」。a little bit concrete 也刻意把要求講小——但對方一旦開口，給的通常遠不只一點點。
questions.pattern: Is there an example of a good [X] that just comes to mind to make this a little bit concrete for people?
questions.episode: Lessons from scaling Ramp | Sri Batchu (Ramp, Instacart, Opendoor)

questions.q: Is there an example you could share when you did that?
questions.zh: 有沒有你真的這樣做過的例子可以分享？
questions.why: when you did that 這五個字是關鍵：不要通則、不要別人的、要你本人做過的那一次。這一刀切下去，對方就沒辦法再用「一般來說我們會……」帶過。
questions.pattern: Is there an example you could share when you did that?
questions.episode: Lessons from scaling Ramp | Sri Batchu (Ramp, Instacart, Opendoor)

questions.q: Is there an example that we could talk about? I know you can't talk about the product you're working on yet, but from the past of a vision that you crafted maybe to share what the vision was or how you came to that to make this even more real?
questions.zh: 有沒有哪個例子我們可以聊？我知道你現在手上的產品還不能講，但有沒有以前做過的願景、可以講講那個願景是什麼、你怎麼想出來的，讓這件事更具體？
questions.why: 先替對方把保密顧慮講出來（I know you can't talk about X yet），對方就不用自己開口拒絕、也不會用「這不方便講」整段擋掉。接著馬上指一條合法的路：改講過去的。
questions.pattern: I know you can't talk about [敏感範圍], but is there an example from the past you could share to make this even more real?
questions.episode: Vision, conviction, and hype: How to build 0 to 1 inside a company | Mihika Kapoor (Product at Figma)

questions.q: Is there an example of a project that comes to mind that was below that bar and then you pushed it above where you're like, "Here's the thing we were missing."?
questions.zh: 有沒有哪個專案是本來達不到那個標準、後來被你推上去的，那種「我們原本就是少了這個」的例子？
questions.why: 他不要「好例子」，他要一個有轉折的例子：先低於標準、後來被推上去。指定了轉折點，對方就不能給你一個從頭到尾都很順的漂亮案例——而轉折點正是所有可學的東西所在。
questions.pattern: Is there an example of [X] that was below that bar and then you pushed it above where you're like, "Here's the thing we were missing"?
questions.episode: Be fundamentally different, not incrementally better | Jag Duggal (Nubank, Facebook, Google, Quantcast)

questions.q: Can you say more on that?
questions.zh: 這個可以再多說一點嗎？
questions.why: 追問裡最省力的一句。不指定方向、不加判斷，等於把麥克風原封不動遞回去，對方會自己挑他覺得最重要的那條線繼續講——常常比你自己設定的方向更值錢。
questions.pattern: Can you say more on that?
questions.episode: Lessons from scaling Uber and Opendoor | Brian Tolkin (Head of Product at Opendoor, ex-Uber)

questions.q: Wait, what do you mean by that?
questions.zh: 等等，你這句是什麼意思？
questions.why: Wait 是合法的打斷器：它把責任講成「我沒跟上」而不是「你講不清楚」。在英文會議裡，聽不懂的當下就喊 wait，比等對方講完再回頭問要自然得多，也不會讓討論白跑十分鐘。
questions.pattern: Wait, what do you mean by that?
questions.episode: The ultimate guide to performance marketing | Timothy Davis (Shopify)

questions.q: Say more about that. What does that look like?
questions.zh: 再多說一點。那實際上長什麼樣子？
questions.why: 兩句一組：第一句要更多，第二句立刻指定形式——不要更多形容詞，要一個可以想像的畫面。單獨用 say more，對方可能只是把同一句話換句話說；加上 what does that look like 才會逼出細節。
questions.pattern: Say more about that. What does that look like?
questions.episode: Lessons from 1,000+ YC startups: Resilience, tar pit ideas, pivoting, more | Dalton Caldwell (Y Combinator, Managing Director)

questions.q: And when you say unconventional, what do you mean?
questions.zh: 你說的「不按牌理」，是指什麼？
questions.why: 只挑出對方剛用的那一個形容詞來問。這種問法有個副作用：對方會意識到自己剛剛用了一個含糊的詞，之後講話會自動變精確。成本只有九個字。
questions.pattern: And when you say [對方的形容詞], what do you mean?
questions.episode: Lessons from Airtable’s unconventional growth strategy | Zoelle Egner

questions.q: I like this phrase that you just use, the loop and not the lane. Can you say more about that?
questions.zh: 我很喜歡你剛剛用的那個說法——「是迴圈，不是車道」。可以再多講一點嗎？
questions.why: 先把對方的原話原封不動引回去，等於告訴他「這句你講得好，值得展開」。被稱讚過的句子，人幾乎一定會願意再解釋一次——而且會解釋得比第一次更用力。
questions.pattern: I like this phrase that you just use, [對方的原話]. Can you say more about that?
questions.episode: How 80,000 companies build with AI: products as organisms, the death of org charts, and why agents will outnumber employees by 2026 | Asha Sharma (CVP of AI Platform at Microsoft)

questions.q: There's so many threads I want to follow here, but maybe on just this last one, when you say taste, what do you mean by that? What should people think when they're like, "Okay, I got to work in my taste"?
questions.zh: 這裡有太多條線我想追了，但先講最後那一條：你說的 taste 是什麼意思？當有人心想「好，我得練我的品味」的時候，他們該想的到底是什麼？
questions.why: 第一句先承認自己想問的很多、然後明確挑一條——這是控制對話節奏的手法，讓對方知道你不是隨機跳題。第二句把問題從「定義」換成「別人聽完該怎麼辦」，把抽象詞逼進可操作的層次。
questions.pattern: There's so many threads I want to follow here, but maybe on just this last one, when you say [X], what do you mean by that?
questions.episode: Thinking like a gardener not a builder, organizing teams like slime mold, the adjacent possible, and other unconventional product advice | Alex Komoroske (Stripe, Google)

questions.q: When you talk about network effects, what does that mean to you? How would you define that briefly?
questions.zh: 你講到網路效應的時候，那對你來說是什麼意思？可以簡短定義一下嗎？
questions.why: 重點在 to you：不是問這個詞的標準定義，是問「你用它的時候指的是什麼」。這一問常會發現兩人講的根本是不同的東西。briefly 則替對方設好長度上限，他就不會怕開口。
questions.pattern: When you talk about [X], what does that mean to you? How would you define that briefly?
questions.episode: How to grow a subscription business | Yuriy Timen (Grammarly, Canva, Airtable)

questions.q: Whoa, say more there. Is the kind of insight there is just things seem like they're 99% done, but they're actually very far from being done?
questions.zh: 哇，這裡再多講一點。你講的重點是不是——事情看起來已經完成 99%，其實離完成還很遠？
questions.why: 先要更多，然後主動丟出自己的理解版本讓對方修正。這比空問「什麼意思」有效：對方要嘛說「對，而且……」，要嘛說「不完全是」然後給你更準的版本——兩條路都會拿到新資訊。
questions.pattern: Whoa, say more there. Is the kind of insight there is just [你的理解版本]?
questions.episode: How Revolut trains world-class product managers: The “local CEO” model, raw intellect over experience, and a cultural obsession with building wow products | Dmitry Zlokazov (Head of Product)

questions.q: And this point that you made that ops is often a sign of inefficiency on a product team because in theory, a lot of the roles should be done by software, eventually. I'd love to unpack this and hear your take on this?
questions.zh: 你剛提到的這一點——營運工作往往是產品團隊沒效率的訊號，因為理論上很多角色最後都該由軟體來做。我想把這個拆開來聽聽你的看法。
questions.why: 第一句把對方的論點完整複述一遍（而且用他的邏輯），第二句才說「我想拆開來看」。先證明你聽懂了再要求展開，對方不會覺得是在被質疑，而是被邀請深講。
questions.pattern: And this point that you made that [完整複述對方論點]. I'd love to unpack this and hear your take on this?
questions.episode: How to sell your ideas and rise within your company | Casey Winters, Eventbrite

questions.q: Can you follow that thread actually? Just when you say that, what does that look like? What are some elements of that process to make this work efficiently?
questions.zh: 這條線可以再追下去嗎？你剛說的那個，實際上長什麼樣？那個流程裡有哪些環節讓它跑得順？
questions.why: 三段式推進：先請求許可（follow that thread），再要畫面（what does that look like），最後要組成元件（what are some elements）。每一句都比前一句更具體，對方會被一路帶到細節層，而不是被一次問死。
questions.pattern: Can you follow that thread actually? Just when you say that, what does that look like? What are some elements of that process?
questions.episode: Behind the product: Duolingo streaks | Jackson Shuttleworth (Group PM, Retention Team)

questions.q: How do you actually get better at that or develop those skills?
questions.zh: 那實際上要怎麼把這個練起來、怎麼養成這些能力？
questions.why: actually 是這句的重心：它暗示前面那段還停在「應該要有」的層次。把問題從「這重要嗎」轉成「怎麼練」，對方就不能再給原則，只能給方法。
questions.pattern: How do you actually get better at that or develop those skills?
questions.episode: How to unlock your product leadership skills | Ken Norton, Ex-Google

questions.q: How do you actually operationalize this without just being overloaded with work and constantly having to meet with every team and remind them of the story?
questions.zh: 這件事實際上要怎麼落地，才不會被工作壓垮、不用一直跟每個團隊開會提醒他們那套說法？
questions.why: 把「執行時會遇到的最大阻力」直接寫進問句裡。這麼一來對方不能只回答理想流程，他必須順帶解掉你提出的那個現實問題——一句話同時要到做法和限制條件。
questions.pattern: How do you actually operationalize this without [執行時最現實的阻力]?
questions.episode: Jeetu Patel

questions.q: And very practically, how do you actually ask people? Is there a little pop-up on the website?
questions.zh: 那很實際地說，你們到底怎麼問使用者？是網站上跳一個小視窗嗎？
questions.why: 先問開放題，再自己補一個很土、很具體的猜測。猜錯反而好：對方會急著糾正你，糾正的過程就會給出真正的做法。這招專治「我們就是會去問使用者啊」這種空答案。
questions.pattern: And very practically, how do you actually [X]? Is there [一個很具體的土猜測]?
questions.episode: How to drive word of mouth | Nilan Peiris (CPO of Wise)

questions.q: And so do you just kind of schedule a meeting, kick it off, point everyone to this Miro doc, for example, with a bunch of prompts and sticky notes and things like that? How do you actually practically do that?
questions.zh: 所以你們就是排一場會、開場、把大家指到那份 Miro 文件、上面一堆提示和便利貼之類的嗎？實際操作上到底怎麼跑？
questions.why: 同一招的加長版：先把整個流程用外行的方式演一遍給對方看，讓他有東西可以修。人很難憑空描述自己的日常流程，但很容易挑出你哪裡講錯了。
questions.pattern: And so do you just kind of [把你猜的流程演一遍]? How do you actually practically do that?
questions.episode: Nickey Skarstad (Airbnb, Etsy, Shopify, Duolingo) on translating vision into goals, operationalizing product quality, second-order decisions, brainstorming, influence, and much more

questions.q: Double click there for a moment. Is that still useful if you're not doing TV and other forms of advertising?
questions.zh: 這裡先深入一下。如果沒有在投電視或其他形式的廣告，這招還有用嗎？
questions.why: Double click 是矽谷會議的固定用語，等於「這一點先放大來看」。後面接的不是「請多說」而是一個限縮條件的假設題——把對方的通則丟進一個他沒設想過的情境，看它會不會破。
questions.pattern: Double click there for a moment. Is that still useful if you're not [對方預設的前提]?
questions.episode: How to grow a subscription business | Yuriy Timen (Grammarly, Canva, Airtable)

questions.q: Say more about that. What have you found helps in creating that sense of urgency and continuing to increase output?
questions.zh: 再多說一點。你發現什麼東西最能製造那種急迫感、讓產出持續往上？
questions.why: say more 之後不是留白，而是接一個 what have you found helps 的問句。found 這個字很關鍵：問的是他實際觀察到有效的東西，不是他認為應該有效的東西。
questions.pattern: Say more about that. What have you found helps in [具體目標]?
questions.episode: Driving alignment and urgency within teams, work-life balance, and the changing PM landscape | Nikita Miller (The Knot, Trello)

questions.q: That is really empowering. Is there anything that helps you build that skill, that's not natural to a lot of people, being okay with failure, and leaning into things that they think they'll probably fail at? Where did that come from, for you?
questions.zh: 這真的很有力量。有什麼東西幫你練出這個能力——就是能接受失敗、願意去做自己覺得多半會搞砸的事，這對很多人並不自然？那對你來說，這是從哪裡來的？
questions.why: 先幫對方把「這件事對多數人不自然」講出來，讓他知道你懂這有多難；最後那句 Where did that come from, for you? 把問題從技巧轉到來源，逼出的通常是一段真實經歷而不是一條建議。
questions.pattern: Is there anything that helps you build that skill, that's not natural to a lot of people? Where did that come from, for you?
questions.episode: Building Wiz: the fastest-growing startup in history | Raaz Herzberg (CMO and VP Product Strategy)

questions.q: Okay, cool. We're going to talk about it, but just maybe you've already answered it, why this is something you're so passionate about, but why this kind of ongoing investment in hardware?
questions.zh: 好，我們等下會談到，不過你可能剛剛已經回答過了——為什麼你對這件事這麼投入？為什麼要持續投資在硬體上？
questions.why: 先給對方一個台階（maybe you've already answered it），再問一個他剛才其實迴避掉的問題。這句免責讓追問聽起來像是自己沒聽仔細，而不是在指控對方閃避——同一個問題問第二次的標準做法。
questions.pattern: Maybe you've already answered it, but why [他剛剛避開的那個問題]?
questions.episode: Snapchat CEO: Why distribution has become the most important moat | Evan Spiegel

questions.q: Something that I've seen happen with larger companies, especially as companies grow, is a little bit of cynicism of user research, specifically how few people you talk to and how that leads to you making a decision. How do you respond to those kinds of concerns?
questions.zh: 我看到大公司、尤其是規模變大之後，對使用者研究會有點犬儒——特別是覺得你只訪了那麼少人，卻拿來下決定。你怎麼回應這類質疑？
questions.why: 把質疑掛在「我看到的現象」上，不是「我覺得」。攻擊面因此落在那些不在場的人身上，對方不必為自己辯護，可以直接處理論點。respond to concerns 也比 defend 溫和，卻同樣要求他正面回答。
questions.pattern: Something that I've seen happen with [場合] is a little bit of cynicism of [對方的主張]. How do you respond to those kinds of concerns?
questions.episode: Teresa Torres on how to interview customers, automating continuous discovery, the opportunity solution tree framework, making the case for user research, common interviewing mistakes, and much more

questions.q: I imagine many people see that, they see Elon, they see Steve Jobs, and the perception is they're very challenge directly people, they're not clearly care about you people, but they're very successful. What do you say to people that are like, but it works. Why wouldn't I be that if that's the way I want to do it?
questions.zh: 我猜很多人看到那些例子——看馬斯克、看賈伯斯——印象就是他們超級直接開幹、又不太在乎人，但他們就是很成功。對那些覺得「可是這招有效啊」的人，你會怎麼說？如果我就想那樣做，為什麼不行？
questions.why: 用反例攻擊對方的框架，但把反例包在「很多人會這樣想」裡。最後一句 Why wouldn't I be that 甚至短暫地站到反方立場——不是為了吵架，是為了逼對方把最強的反駁講出來。
questions.pattern: I imagine many people see [反例], and the perception is [反例的邏輯]. What do you say to people that are like, but it works?
questions.episode: Radical Candor: From theory to practice with author Kim Scott

questions.q: And so, what is this a reaction to? Because I imagine many people hearing this are, like, "Of course, PMs, product teams we're driving business impact, well, that's why we're here."
questions.zh: 所以這是在反應什麼？因為我猜很多人聽到會想：「產品經理、產品團隊本來就是在推動商業成效啊，我們不就是為這個而存在的嗎？」
questions.why: 先問「你這主張是在反抗什麼」——這一問把對方的立場放回它的脈絡，逼他說出對手是誰。第二句再幫聽眾把最直覺的反駁講出來，讓對方非回應不可，而反駁的人是「很多人」不是你。
questions.pattern: And so, what is this a reaction to? Because I imagine many people hearing this are like, "[最直覺的反駁]"
questions.episode: The one question that saves product careers | Matt LeMay

questions.q: I imagine some people hearing this advice are going to feel like, "I'm not going to get a job at OpenAI or Glean or other awesome companies that everyone wants to go work at." Any advice to those folks?
questions.zh: 我猜有些人聽到這個建議會覺得：「我又進不去 OpenAI 或 Glean 那種大家都想去的好公司。」對這些人你有什麼建議？
questions.why: 代替聽眾提出「我做不到」的異議。這種問法不否定對方的建議，而是指出它的適用範圍——結果通常會逼出一個更務實、對一般人真的可用的版本。
questions.pattern: I imagine some people hearing this advice are going to feel like, "[做不到的理由]" Any advice to those folks?
questions.episode: Lessons in product leadership and AI strategy from Glean, Google, Amazon, and Slack | Tamar Yehoshua (Product at Glean, ex-Google and Slack)

questions.q: I imagine many people listening to this or feeling like, I wish I could not be in these dumb meetings that I'm in all the time and these stupid reviews. And there's a lot of stuff you have no control over that also are very energy zapping. What advice would you give to people thinking that?
questions.zh: 我猜很多聽的人心裡在想：真希望我不用一直坐在那些沒意義的會、那些爛 review 裡。而且有一堆事你根本控制不了，卻一直在耗你的能量。對這樣想的人你會給什麼建議？
questions.why: 先把聽眾的抱怨完整說出來（包括情緒），再要建議。把異議演到位、連語氣都學起來，對方就無法用一句通則打發——因為他得先回應那個具體處境。
questions.pattern: I imagine many people listening to this are feeling like, [完整演出他們的抱怨]. What advice would you give to people thinking that?
questions.episode: How to discover your superpowers, own your story, and unlock personal growth | Donna Lichaw (author of The Leader’s Journey)

questions.q: I wanted to come back to the burnout piece. I imagine some folks are listening to this and they're like, "Am I burnt out? I don't know." What are signs that you're burnt out versus just working a lot and tired?
questions.zh: 我想回到 burnout 那段。我猜有些人正在聽、心裡想「我是不是 burnout 了？我也不知道。」怎麼分辨自己是真的 burnout，還是只是工作太多、很累？
questions.why: 重點是最後那個 versus。與其問「怎麼判斷 X」，不如給出一個很容易被混淆的對照組，逼對方畫出分界線。要定義的時候拿不到東西，要分界線通常就拿得到。
questions.pattern: What are signs that you're [X] versus just [容易混淆的另一種狀況]?
questions.episode: When and how to invest in new acquisition channels | Adam Grenier (Uber, MasterClass)

questions.q: Most people hearing this assume they are barrels. What helps you understand if someone's truly a barrel?
questions.zh: 大部分聽到這段的人都會覺得自己是那個「桶子」。你怎麼判斷一個人是不是真的是？
questions.why: 先點破一個集體盲點——每個人都覺得自己是好的那一類——再要判準。這樣問等於預先否決了對方給出「自我感覺良好就算」的答案，他必須給外部可驗證的訊號。
questions.pattern: Most people hearing this assume they are [好的那一類]. What helps you understand if someone's truly [那一類]?
questions.episode: Hard truths about building in the AI era | Keith Rabois (Khosla Ventures)

questions.q: So in a lot of decks it's like, "Oh, we have the most amazing team. We move the fastest." You mention how rarely is that actually a power?
questions.zh: 很多簡報上都會寫「我們團隊超強、我們跑得最快」。你提到這其實很少真的構成一種優勢？
questions.why: 先舉一個所有人都做過的普遍行為，再用對方自己說過的話把它打掉。You mention 這三個字很重要：反駁的來源是對方本人，你只是把它拿出來對準現場——衝突值歸零，力道不變。
questions.pattern: So in a lot of [場合] it's like, "[大家都在講的話]". You mention how rarely is that actually [X]?
questions.episode: Business strategy with Hamilton Helmer (author of 7 Powers)

questions.q: Just to push back, I imagine there are expectations of like, "I hope this works out. I hope people adopt it. I hope it becomes the best email client in town." There's a sense of like, "We want this to succeed"?
questions.zh: 純粹想反駁一下：我猜還是有期待的吧，像是「希望這個能成、希望大家會用、希望它變成市面上最好的 email 工具」。多少還是有一種「我們想讓它成功」的感覺吧？
questions.why: Just to push back 是英文會議裡最安全的反駁開場：先宣告接下來這句是唱反調，對方就知道這是角色扮演不是攻擊。接著不是講道理，而是直接演出對方心裡可能有的話，讓他去否認或承認。
questions.pattern: Just to push back, I imagine there are [對方否認過的東西], like "[演出對方的心聲]". There's a sense of like [X]?
questions.episode: Jason Fried challenges your thinking on fundraising, goals, growth, and more

questions.q: Your advice here is that doesn't work?
questions.zh: 所以你的建議是，那招沒用？
questions.why: 把對方一長段委婉的說法壓縮成一句最直白的結論，然後丟回去讓他確認。他要嘛點頭（你就拿到一句可引用的強論述），要嘛急著修正（你就拿到他真正的分寸）。七個字，兩條路都贏。
questions.pattern: Your advice here is that [最直白的結論]?
questions.episode: Sequoia CEO coach: Why it’s never been easier to start a company, and never been harder to scale one | Brian Halligan (co-founder, HubSpot)

questions.q: But you're saying that actually is what you do and that actually works really well?
questions.zh: 但你的意思是，你們真的就是這樣做，而且效果真的很好？
questions.why: But you're saying 帶著明顯的不可置信，但形式上仍是請對方確認而不是否定他。這種「重述＋懷疑」是最低成本的挑戰：如果對方剛才誇大了，這一問會讓他自己往回收。
questions.pattern: But you're saying that actually is what you do and that actually works really well?
questions.episode: Linear’s secret to building beloved B2B products | Nan Yu (Head of Product)

questions.q: I know that you have this pretty spicy contrarian take on experimentation and that I think you believe people run experiments too often and maybe not everything should be an experiment. Can you talk about that?
questions.zh: 我知道你對實驗有個蠻嗆的反主流看法——你好像認為大家做實驗做得太頻繁，不是每件事都該拿去做實驗。可以談談這個嗎？
questions.why: 他不是自己去挑戰對方，而是把對方最有爭議的立場先講白、貼上 contrarian 的標籤，再請他辯護。先命名爭議，對話就從「你同不同意」變成「你來論證」，主導權在你手上。
questions.pattern: I know that you have this pretty spicy contrarian take on [主題], that you believe [具爭議的立場]. Can you talk about that?
questions.episode: Mastering onboarding | Lauryn Isford (Head of Growth at Airtable)

questions.q: There's obviously a bit of overhead and downside to running an experiment, setting all up, and analyzing the results. Is there anything that you ever don't think is worth A/B testing?
questions.zh: 做實驗顯然有一些額外成本和代價——要設定、要分析結果。有沒有什麼是你認為根本不值得做 A/B 測試的？
questions.why: 對一個以此成名的專家，問他「有沒有不適用的時候」。第一句先自己說出成本，代表你不是外行在唱反調。這一問幾乎一定會拿到比整段訪談都有用的邊界條件。
questions.pattern: There's obviously a bit of overhead and downside to [對方的方法]. Is there anything that you ever don't think is worth [那個方法]?
questions.episode: The ultimate guide to A/B testing | Ronny Kohavi (Airbnb, Microsoft, Amazon)

questions.q: Is there something you've done in building your company that has been counter to that, something you've learned about? Because I totally agree, people always talk about team, team, team and then that's often really sucky to work at a lot of companies and clearly they don't care that much about your experience.
questions.zh: 在你自己建立公司的過程中，有沒有哪件事是跟那個說法反著來的、你學到什麼？因為我完全同意——大家老是把「團隊、團隊、團隊」掛嘴上，可是那些公司待起來往往很糟，顯然他們根本沒那麼在乎你的感受。
questions.why: counter to that 直接向對方索取反例——不是問他同不同意，是問他哪裡違反了通說。第二句用 I totally agree 站到對方那一邊，讓這個反例聽起來像是兩人一起拆別人的假話。
questions.pattern: Is there something you've done in [領域] that has been counter to that, something you've learned about?
questions.episode: 10 lessons on bootstrapping a $200m business | Patrick Campbell (ProfitWell)

questions.q: It doesn't feel intuitive to go after small markets and to find niches. So let's just follow that thread. Well, why is that actually a source of some of the best ideas starting really small and niche?
questions.zh: 去做小市場、去找利基，感覺其實不太直覺。那就順著這條線講下去吧——為什麼從很小、很利基的地方開始，反而是最好點子的來源之一？
questions.why: 第一句就把「這聽起來不合理」講出來，替所有心裡有疑問的人擋在前面。承認不直覺，等於要求對方補上論證，而不是重複他的結論。actually 這個字則暗示：請解釋反直覺的機制。
questions.pattern: It doesn't feel intuitive to [對方的主張]. Why is that actually [他宣稱的好處]?
questions.episode: I’ve run 75+ businesses. Here’s why you’re probably chasing the wrong idea. | Andrew Wilkinson (co‑founder of Tiny)

questions.q: What I'm hearing from a meta point you're making is use that ask as leverage to change the way things are operating. Is that right?
questions.zh: 我聽到的、更上一層的意思是：把那個請求當成槓桿，去改變事情運作的方式。是這樣嗎？
questions.why: 不重述對方的字面內容，而是往上抽一層講出他沒明說的原則，再問「是這樣嗎」。猜對，你替他把話講得更漂亮；猜錯，他會親自修正——這是把模糊發言逼成明確立場最有禮貌的方法。
questions.pattern: What I'm hearing from a meta point you're making is [往上抽一層的原則]. Is that right?
questions.episode: Velocity over everything: How Ramp became the fastest-growing SaaS startup of all time | Geoff Charles (VP of Product)

questions.q: Okay. What are maybe the most common mistakes they make that aren't as obvious?
questions.zh: 好。那他們最常犯、但比較沒那麼明顯的錯是什麼？
questions.why: 關鍵在 that aren't as obvious：先把「大家都知道的那些錯」排除掉，對方就不能給你網路上查得到的答案。同樣一個問題，加這五個字，答案的等級直接跳一層。
questions.pattern: What are maybe the most common mistakes they make that aren't as obvious?
questions.episode: Relentless curiosity, radical accountability, and HubSpot’s winning growth formula | Christopher Miller (VP of Product, Growth and AI)

questions.q: So, I thought we'd start with Make Time and then get to Sprint in the second half of the conversation. First question is just what do most people get wrong when they're trying to become more productive?
questions.zh: 我想先從《Make Time》開始，下半場再談《Sprint》。第一個問題就是：大家想讓自己更有生產力的時候，最常搞錯的是什麼？
questions.why: 問「大家最常搞錯什麼」而不是「該怎麼做」。錯誤比正解具體、也比較好舉例，而且對方講錯誤時通常會順帶把正解說出來——等於一問拿兩份。
questions.pattern: What do most people get wrong when they're trying to [目標]?
questions.episode: Making time for what matters | Jake Knapp and John Zeratsky (authors of Sprint and Make Time, co-founders of Character Capital)

questions.q: What are some of the most common mistakes that PMs make early on in their career that hurt their career?
questions.zh: 產品經理在職涯早期最常犯、而且真的會傷到職涯的錯有哪些？
questions.why: 在「常見錯誤」後面加了一道篩子：that hurt their career。有了後果條件，對方就不會給你無傷大雅的小毛病清單，只能挑真正有代價的那幾個。
questions.pattern: What are some of the most common mistakes that [角色] make early on in their career that hurt their career?
questions.episode: Jackie Bavaro on getting better at product strategy, what exactly is strategy, PM pitfalls to avoid, advancing your career, getting into management, and much more

questions.q: If you kind of zoomed out a little bit and thought about the startups you've worked with, what would you say are the most common mistakes that early stage startups make broadly?
questions.zh: 如果你稍微拉遠一點、想想你合作過的那些新創，你會說早期新創最常犯的錯大概是什麼？
questions.why: 先請對方拉遠視角（zoomed out）再問錯誤，會拿到「模式」而不是某一家公司的八卦。thought about the startups you've worked with 又把範圍鎖回他的親身樣本，避免變成泛泛的產業評論。
questions.pattern: If you zoomed out a little bit and thought about [他的樣本], what would you say are the most common mistakes that [對象] make broadly?
questions.episode: Gustaf Alstromer

questions.q: So let's go to the other side of this question. We talked about what mistakes new PMs make. I'm curious, what's the biggest product mistake that you've made?
questions.zh: 那我們換到問題的另一面。剛剛談的是新手 PM 會犯什麼錯，我很好奇——你自己犯過最大的產品錯誤是什麼？
questions.why: 兩段式：先問通則（別人會犯的錯），再突然把槍口轉向本人。第一問讓對方進入「談錯誤」的模式，第二問才難以閃避——如果一開場就問「你犯過什麼錯」，多半只會拿到公關答案。
questions.pattern: We talked about what mistakes [別人] make. I'm curious, what's the biggest [X] mistake that you've made?
questions.episode: Building minimum lovable products, stories from WeWork and Airbnb, and thriving as a PM | Jiaona Zhang (Webflow, WeWork, Airbnb, Dropbox)

questions.q: What's a story that comes to mind when you think about your biggest mistake?
questions.zh: 講到你犯過最大的錯，有沒有哪個故事會浮上心頭？
questions.why: 不問「錯誤」，問「故事」。一講故事就得有時間地點人物，對方沒辦法用一句抽象的教訓帶過。comes to mind 又暗示不用挑最嚴重的，第一個想到的就好。
questions.pattern: What's a story that comes to mind when you think about your biggest mistake?
questions.episode: He saved OpenAI, invented the “Like” button, and built Google Maps: Bret Taylor on the future of careers, coding, agents, and more

questions.q: Along those same lines, is there a misconception of Lean Startup or any of the other things you put out that just really frustrates you, that just is a recurring misconception that people just continue to get wrong?
questions.zh: 同樣的脈絡下，關於精實創業、或你提出過的其他東西，有沒有哪個誤解真的讓你很不爽、大家一直重複弄錯的？
questions.why: 問「誤解」而不是「錯誤」，把對方放在受害者而不是被告的位置。再加上 that just really frustrates you——邀請情緒，而情緒會帶出最具體、最不客套的例子。
questions.pattern: Is there a misconception of [對方的作品／方法] that just really frustrates you, that people just continue to get wrong?
questions.episode: Reflections on a movement | Eric Ries (creator of the Lean Startup methodology)

questions.q: What's a sign that maybe it's not working out when you hire your either first salesperson or maybe first five, what are signs? Because you said it often does not work out, what are early signals like, "We should rethink this"?
questions.zh: 在你請第一個業務、或前五個業務的時候，有什麼跡象代表這件事其實不太順？因為你說這常常不會成功——有哪些早期訊號在講「我們該重新想一下」？
questions.why: 不問「為什麼會失敗」，問「失敗前有什麼徵兆」。原因是事後諸葛，徵兆才是現場能用的。第二句還把對方剛才講過的話（it often does not work out）拿回來當提問的理由。
questions.pattern: What's a sign that maybe it's not working out when you [做某事]? What are early signals like, "We should rethink this"?
questions.episode: Founder-led sales | Pete Kazanjy (Founding Sales, Atrium)

questions.q: How do you know if it's the creative that is failing versus it's just never going to work? Is there something that tells you that's what's not working?
questions.zh: 你怎麼分辨是素材本身有問題、還是這條路本來就走不通？有沒有什麼東西會告訴你到底是哪裡不對？
questions.why: 把「失敗」拆成兩種原因並要求對方分辨。這種 A versus B 的問法會逼出診斷方法而不是感想——而診斷方法正是別人能帶走的東西。
questions.pattern: How do you know if it's [原因A] that is failing versus it's just [原因B]?
questions.episode: The ultimate guide to performance marketing | Timothy Davis (Shopify)

questions.q: Yeah, absolutely. How do you know when it's probably a bad idea to try to create your own category?
questions.zh: 對，完全同意。那你怎麼判斷，什麼時候做這件事其實是個爛主意？
questions.why: 問「什麼時候這是壞主意」是最好用的邊界追問：對方剛講完一套方法，這一問直接要他畫出方法的失效範圍。而且用 probably a bad idea 而不是 wrong，語氣軟，殺傷力不變。
questions.pattern: How do you know when it's probably a bad idea to [做某事]?
questions.episode: Category creation and brand building | Barbra Gago (Pando, Miro, Greenhouse, Culture Amp)

questions.q: Along these lines of just bad ideas, things people shouldn't start, what are a few ideas that you think everyone thinks is going to be a great idea and then they do it and then they always fail?
questions.zh: 順著爛點子這條線講——有哪幾種點子是大家都覺得一定會紅，結果做下去每次都倒？
questions.why: 把問題設計成「共識和現實相反」的那一格：不是問什麼會失敗，是問什麼看起來很好卻總是失敗。這種問法一定會問出反直覺的答案，因為問題本身就排除了顯而易見的選項。
questions.pattern: What are a few ideas that you think everyone thinks is going to be a great idea and then they do it and then they always fail?
questions.episode: I’ve run 75+ businesses. Here’s why you’re probably chasing the wrong idea. | Andrew Wilkinson (co‑founder of Tiny)

questions.q: What do you find is often the biggest mistake that founders make when they're trying to hire their first senior product leader?
questions.zh: 你觀察下來，創辦人在找第一位資深產品主管的時候，最常犯的最大錯誤是什麼？
questions.why: What do you find 把問題定錨在對方的實際觀察，而不是他的意見。再把場景壓到一個很窄的情境（第一位、資深、產品主管），窄場景會逼出具體答案，寬問題只會換來廢話。
questions.pattern: What do you find is often the biggest mistake that [對象] make when they're trying to [具體情境]?
questions.episode: Lessons from one of the world’s top executive recruiters | Lauren Ipsen (Daversa Partners, General Catalyst)

questions.q: Okay, I'm going to take us to two recurring corners on the podcast, Fail Corner and Hot Seat Corner. Fail Corner, what's something that you worked on that was just a huge failure that helped you become better?
questions.zh: 好，我要帶大家進入節目的兩個固定單元：失敗角落和烤問角落。失敗角落——有沒有哪件你做過的事是徹底失敗、但讓你變得更好的？
questions.why: 先宣告這是一個固定單元，把「談失敗」變成流程而不是針對他個人。that helped you become better 則預先給了失敗一個正當出口，對方才願意講真的。
questions.pattern: What's something that you worked on that was just a huge failure that helped you become better?
questions.episode: Adam Mosseri: AI is a tailwind for authenticity

questions.q: Awesome. Going back to discovery and interviewing, I definitely wanted to ask you what are, I don't know, two or three tips and best practices for interviewing/what are two or three things people usually do wrong that they should try to avoid?
questions.zh: 回到探索和訪談這塊，我很想問：有沒有兩三個訪談的訣竅和最佳做法，或者說，有沒有兩三件大家通常會做錯、應該避免的事？
questions.why: 同一句話裡給了正反兩種問法，讓對方挑好講的那邊回答。而且指定「兩三個」——給數量比不給好，對方會自動排序挑最強的，也不會講到失控。
questions.pattern: What are two or three tips and best practices for [X], or what are two or three things people usually do wrong that they should try to avoid?
questions.episode: Teresa Torres on how to interview customers, automating continuous discovery, the opportunity solution tree framework, making the case for user research, common interviewing mistakes, and much more

questions.q: Awesome. One last question about naming. What's a common mistake that people make going through this process coming up with a name?
questions.zh: 太好了。關於命名，最後一個問題：大家跑這個流程、想名字的時候，最常犯的錯是什麼？
questions.why: 用 one last question 標示這是本段最後一問，對方會知道可以把壓箱寶拿出來。收尾用「最常犯的錯」是很划算的一題——它逼對方把整段內容反過來再講一次重點。
questions.pattern: One last question about [主題]. What's a common mistake that people make going through this process?
questions.episode: The art of building legendary brands | Arielle Jackson (Google, Square, Marketer in Residence at First Round Capital)

questions.q: One final question around the actual OKR document. What do you find are the most one or two common mistakes people make when writing out the objective or the key result in deciding on what to go with?
questions.zh: 關於 OKR 文件本身，最後一個問題：你看到大家在寫目標或關鍵結果、在決定要挑什麼的時候，最常犯的一兩個錯是什麼？
questions.why: the most one or two 是明確的數量上限：對方不會給你一份十點清單，而會被迫排序、只留最痛的。追問時給數量，等於同時要到了答案和優先順序。
questions.pattern: What do you find are the most one or two common mistakes people make when [具體動作]?
questions.episode: The ultimate guide to OKRs | Christina Wodtke (Stanford)
